terms.def: Designing and building so people with physical disabilities can use a building, following the federal ADA Standards, HUD rules, Building Code Chapter 11 and Appendices E, N and P, and/or ICC/ANSI A117.1.

A commercial business such as an adult bookstore, adult-only eating or drinking place or adult theater (or a combination) that regularly features sexually explicit films or images. Some also offer live entertainment where patrons are exposed to specified anatomical areas of the staff.

A project that always results in a new or amended Certificate of Occupancy. It may involve a substantial enlargement or reduction of the building, or a major change to its entrance or exit, zoning use group and/or Building Code occupancy.

Using proper fasteners to support and secure structural members (wall, column, deck, post or beam), fixtures and equipment. Anything supported by an exterior wall must be positively anchored to the main structure and designed for vertical and lateral loads.
Facade elements such as cornices, moldings and facade sculpture that, on older buildings, may project into the public right of way.
Hard-burnt clay, glazed or unglazed, used as cladding or veneer on exterior walls. It can be plain or ornamental, machine-extruded or hand-modeled, and is usually larger than brick or facing tile.
A space below grade next to a building that is open to the outside air and enclosed by walls.

An encroachment a governing agency such as DOB or DOT allows without a special permit or variance. For example, under the Building Code, architectural details may project no more than three inches into the public right of way as-of-right.
Lighting fixtures and devices attached to a building facade.
A projection wholly supported by the building it is attached to, made of a lightweight frame with a covering, that provides weather protection, identity or decoration.
An above-grade extension on the outside of a building, enclosed by a wall or railing (balustrade), reached from an occupied space.

A story partly below curb level but with at least half its height above curb level. Where every part of the building is set back more than 25 feet from a street line, height is measured from adjoining final grade, taken at 10-foot intervals around the exterior walls. A basement counts as a story when measuring height.
A board with power to modify the Zoning Resolution after review and a public hearing. An approved BSA resolution with BSA-stamped plans is required before DOB will review the application (ZR 72-00).
A vertical extension of the exterior wall at the edge of a roof, terrace, balcony, walkway or other structure that acts as a safety barrier.

Installing, modifying or upgrading building systems such as plumbing, boiler, sprinkler, standpipe, fire alarm, HVAC and fire suppression. If the work modifies these systems, the alteration's scope of work must include them.

A permanent, rigid projection with a covering that provides weather protection, identity or decoration. It must be structurally independent, or attached to a building at one end and supported by at least one post (stanchion) at the outer end.

An exterior wall, usually masonry, with an outer and inner layer of brick (wythe) separated by a continuous air space and tied together with wire or sheet-metal ties. The air space provides insulation.

An enclosed space with more than half its height below curb level. Where every part of the building is set back more than 25 feet from a street line, height is measured from adjoining final grade at 10-foot intervals around the exterior walls. A cellar is not counted as a story.

Issued (new or amended) when a project changes a building's occupancy or use, or otherwise affects the existing C of O, for example adding a full story or changing commercial use to residential (AC 28-118.3). DOB may also issue a Partial C of O for part of a building, or a Temporary C of O for a limited time while final inspections or surveys are outstanding (AC 28-118.16).
A protective or insulating layer fixed to the exterior walls of a building or other structure.

A request to the Borough Commissioner's office about a plan examiner's objection, or a possible objection on an application not yet filed (pre-determination). File a ZRD1 (zoning) or CCD1 (Construction Code) form, signed and sealed by a professional. Each form is limited to one request and must cite all related Code or Zoning sections.

A quality assurance testing process that verifies and documents that selected building systems were designed, installed and work according to the owner's requirements, construction documents and minimum Code. It is mandatory when permitted equipment exceeds a total heating capacity of 600 kBTU/h.
Under the Zoning Resolution, a change of use. A use is any purpose for which a building, structure or open land is designed, arranged, maintained or occupied.

A protective cap on top of a wall, parapet, pilaster or chimney, often stone, terracotta, concrete, metal or wood. It may be flat, sloped, double-beveled or curved to shed water and protect the masonry below.
A projection that crowns or finishes part of a building, typically the exterior trim where roof meets wall, usually made of bed molding, soffit, fascia and crown molding.
A concrete border along the roadway that forms the sidewalk edge, which may need a steel face or a row of joined stones.
An angled cut in the sidewalk edge that lets vehicles reach a driveway, garage, parking lot, loading dock or drive-through.

For measuring building height under the Zoning Resolution and Multiple Dwelling Law: the curb level at the center of the building's front, or the average across fronts if the building faces more than one street. Where no curb elevation exists, it is the average final grade around the exterior walls (taken every 10 feet), unless the city engineer sets it.
The line along the face of the street curb next to the roadway.
The outer skin of a building: a non-load-bearing wall of glass, metal or masonry attached to the building's structural frame.
Generally, the maximum floor area allowed on a zoning lot. When less is built than allowed, the difference is unused development rights, often called air rights.
A sidewalk with different material, color, scoring and/or dimensions than DOT's standard sidewalk. Distinctive sidewalks require Public Design Commission (PDC) approval.

Storm water on the sidewalk and roadway along a property must drain into a street drainage system. Storm water falling on-site, as DEP allows, goes to an on-site drywell or similar, or connects to the storm water system or Green Infrastructure at the street.
Any building or structure, or part of one, occupied in whole or in part as the home, residence or sleeping place of one or more people.
Raising a building so its lowest occupied floor is above flood levels shown on FEMA flood maps, as described in Building Code Appendix G and Zoning Resolution Article VI, Chapter 4.
Parts of a building that intrude onto a sidewalk and/or street, including vaults, steps, stoops, footings, fences and retaining walls.

Under the Zoning Resolution: adding floor area to an existing building or zoning lot, or expanding a use into an area not previously used for it. Under the Building Code: any addition of gross floor area to a building.

Moving earth, rock or other material with tools, equipment or explosives, including earthwork, trenching, wall shafts and tunneling. Under BC 3302.1 it is removing earth from its natural position, except incidental removal during augering, drilling, vibrating or driving. Coordination with FDNY is required.
The exterior wall of a building, often used to install antennas.
Building parts made of non-combustible materials with fire-resistance ratings at least equal to those required for the same parts of a fireproof dwelling.

The base of a building, typically concrete with wood or steel structural elements driven into the ground or cast in place. It may be a mat foundation, a slab-on-grade, or individual or strip footings.

Under Multiple Dwelling Law Article 7B, gross floor area is measured to the outside of exterior walls and includes shafts, stairways and similar spaces. Clear (interior) floor area is measured to the interior finished wall surfaces, typically within a room or unit.
A dwelling whose exterior walls, or any structural parts of them, are made of wood.

Group H occupancy covers using a building, or part of one, to manufacture, process, generate or store materials that are a physical or health hazard in excess quantities (BC Tables 307(1) and 307(2)). Zoning Use Group 18 addresses hazardous materials.

A Loft Building meeting the criteria in MDL Section 281, as decided by the Loft Board. Under MDL 280, IMDs are treated as lawfully existing multiple dwellings even if legalization (the process to reach compliance and get a Certificate of Occupancy) has not started.

terms.term: Joint Living Work Quarters for Artists (JLWQA)
terms.def: A type of loft unit under MDL Article 7B, Zoning Use Group 17D, for artists: people regularly engaged in the fine, performing or creative arts and certified by the City's Department of Cultural Affairs and/or the State Council on the Arts.
Changes to a floor layout that add, move, remodel, enlarge or shrink interior rooms while keeping the same building envelope.

terms.term: Letter of No Objection (for units under the Loft Law)
terms.def: A letter (LNO) the owner must get from the Loft Board before obtaining a permit for other work in the building that is not directly related to the IMD unit(s).

Older term, replaced by Place of Assembly Certificate of Operation in the 2008 NYC Building Code. Under the 1938 Code it identified assembly spaces whose lawful use depended on a license from the Fire Department, Police Department or Department of Licenses.
A horizontal structural member, such as a beam, over a door or window opening that carries the wall above. Usually steel, precast concrete, stone or wood.

A building or space designed for commercial or manufacturing use, generally built before 1930. In certain manufacturing districts, lofts may be converted to residential use by City Planning Commission special permit.

The New York City Loft Board, a nine-member board appointed by the Mayor, created by the State Legislature in 1982 to regulate converting certain commercial and manufacturing buildings to lawful residential use.

Before a permit for work to legalize IMD unit(s), once owner and occupants resolve all objections and issues, the Loft Board issues a letter certifying compliance with all Loft Board requirements and stating it has no objections.

Windows in an exterior wall on a side or rear zoning or tax lot line. They require special Code review, based on building type and construction class, to set allowable window size, number and fire protection.

An existing building 10 or more stories or 125 feet or more tall, or with a footprint of 100,000 square feet or more regardless of height, or one the Commissioner designates because of unique construction or demolition hazards.
Under the Zoning Resolution, a building used partly for residential use and partly for community facility and/or commercial use.
Under the Building Code, a building containing two or more occupancy classifications, which may or may not match the zoning use groups. The DOB glossary gives the same definition for Mixed Use.

A single pole that supports an antenna or sign, typically 50 to 120 feet tall but variable. Code requires it be bolted to or embedded in a concrete foundation sized to resist the loads on the structure.
Mesh with side ropes, ties and other parts, installed on scaffolding at construction sites, especially high-rises, to protect pedestrians and workers from falling debris.
A project for a permanent enclosed structure on a plot of land, with a roof and windows, used for any of many activities.

A lawfully existing building or structure that does not comply with applicable bulk regulations, either as of December 15, 1961 or because of a later zoning amendment. Non-compliance means failing to meet any bulk regulation.

Under ZR 12-10, any lawful use of a building that does not conform to one or more use regulations of its zoning district, either on permitted Use Groups or performance standards. Existing non-conforming uses may remain under ZR 52-00.
The purpose or activity a building or space is used for, or is designed, arranged or intended to be used for.
The use as defined in the Building Code: the purpose or activity a building or space is used for, or is designed, arranged or intended to be used for.
The number of people a building's (or part of a building's) exits (means of egress) are designed for.
A building designed and occupied for residence on a long-term basis (more than a month at a time) by no more than one family, as required by the Housing Maintenance Code.
A building designed and occupied for residence on a long-term basis (more than a month at a time) by no more than two families, as required by the Housing Maintenance Code.

When occupants exceed the number on the Certificate of Occupancy or allowed by BC 1004.1. FDNY may also find a safety threat from the number of people, or from people sitting or standing where they block access to exits, aisles, corridors or stairways.
A continuous extension of the exterior wall built entirely above the roof.

Construction that removes, replaces or repairs load-bearing or non-load-bearing interior partitions, changes structural elements inside or out, or changes the facade, while keeping the existing structure.

terms.term: Penalties for Work Without a Permit
terms.def: Doing work without a permit can lead to violations, court appearances and civil or criminal penalties. Some minor alterations, ordinary repairs, and replacing faucets, toilets and sinks need no permit and may be done by someone without a license (AC 28-105.4).
Rectangular or semicircular projections from a wall that reinforce it or act as simulated pillars at entrances and doorways; they may also project from the exterior wall.

A project cannot begin until its plans are reviewed and approved by a DOB Plan Examiner, or accepted if Professionally Certified. Disapproved applications get objections that must be resolved before approval; the design professional schedules appointments with examiners to resolve them.

Occupancy classifications for gatherings of 75 people or more for civic, social or religious functions, recreation, eating or drinking, awaiting transportation or similar group activities. A Place of Assembly Certificate of Operation is required.

terms.term: Place of Assembly Certificate of Operation (PACO)
terms.def: After plans are approved under BC 1028.1.3 and DOB inspection is passed, an initial PACO is issued for one year. After that, an annual FDNY inspection is required to renew it (FC 105.6).

A raised area in a building for worship, music, plays or entertainment, a head table, lecturers and speakers, boxing and wrestling rings, theater-in-the-round and similar uses, with no overhead curtains, drops, scenery or stage effects other than lighting and sound. A temporary platform is installed for no more than 30 days.
Pointing is the mortar in the joints between bricks, stone and other masonry units; repointing is removing old mortar and replacing it with new.
A DOB violation where a Notice of Violation, administrative summons, criminal court summons or other process was issued before the initial work permit was issued.

An amenity the property owner provides and maintains for public use, usually in exchange for extra floor area. Mostly in Manhattan's high-density central business districts, typically an arcade or public plaza with seating and landscaping, inside or outside a building.
The legal boundary (metes and bounds) of a parcel of land.

Submitting construction documents prepared by a registered design professional (Professional Engineer or Registered Architect) to DOB for approval. In some cases, with the owner's consent, the professional may self-certify Code compliance (professional certification) instead of DOB review.

To close a permit, the owner, applicant or contractor must have the finished work inspected for final sign-off and submit a work completion notification to DOB. In some cases a letter of completion may be issued.

A privately owned open area next to a building and open to the public, generally at the level of the adjoining sidewalk and open to the sky except for seating and other permitted amenities. In some high-density districts a floor area bonus is available for providing one.
The public street space beyond the private property line, including roadway and sidewalk.
Open space outside a building that is dedicated to public use by lawful mapping or another lawful procedure.
A person licensed and registered to practice land surveying under New York State education law.

Changes to an existing building, such as remodeling or replacing outdated or damaged structures and materials, partial demolition of interior partitions, and installing or replacing building systems or equipment as regular maintenance. Renovations do not affect exits, change the use, or increase the occupant load.

Building Code: Group R is use for dwelling or sleeping; three or more units make a multiple dwelling under the Multiple Dwelling Law; stays may be transient (30 days or less) or non-transient. Zoning Resolution: a building with one or more dwelling or rooming units, excluding hotels and community facilities with sleeping space; also a district type where hotels are not allowed.

A wall that holds back soil between two elevations, resisting lateral forces from soil, rock, water or other materials (BC 1801.3). Basement walls and vault walls of buildings and underground structures, such as utility vaults, tunnels and transit stations, are not retaining walls.
Under City Charter Chapter 14, Section 362(d), a right the City can revoke at any time, allowing private use or improvements on, over or under City streets and sidewalks. DOT has jurisdiction.

An enclosed space running through one or more stories (or to the roof) connecting a series of openings, whether for air, light, elevator, dumbwaiter, enclosed stairway or other purpose, interior or exterior.
Any covered space below a sidewalk and/or street, except openings used only for steps down to a building's cellar or basement.

A Site Safety Plan is required for major buildings, including new buildings, alterations and demolitions 10 stories or more, and facade work on buildings 15 stories or more (BC 3310). It details construction logistics protecting public areas and neighbors, such as fences, sidewalk sheds, adjoining buildings and safety netting (AC 28-110.1).

A temporary or permanent building for amusement, entertainment or education with a walkway, or a ride that carries passengers around or over a course (for example haunted houses, laser tag arenas, mazes). Exits may not be obvious because of visual or audio distractions or an intentionally confusing path.

Inspections of selected materials, equipment, installation, fabrication and connections to confirm they match approved construction documents and standards. Only DOB-registered Special Inspection Agencies (SIAs), their representatives or qualified professionals may perform them.
Storm water from all water-resistant surfaces on a property must drain into a public storm or combined sewer, or an on-site private disposal system such as a drywell.
A space in a building for entertainment or presentations that has overhead curtains, drops, scenery or stage effects other than lighting and sound.
Temporary, seasonal vestibules allowed as supplementary building entrances.

A floor level of a building, significant under both Code and Zoning. Adding a third story to a one- or two-family home could trigger more fire protection requirements. Basements are stories, cellars are not, and an attic may be considered a story.
The lot line fronting a street, separating the street from other land.
An exterior wall or facade of a building at the street line.
A tract of property on the City's tax map on which property taxes are assessed.

Moving unused development rights from one zoning lot to another in limited cases, usually to preserve historic buildings, open space or cultural resources, where a zoning lot merger is not possible. For a landmark, City Planning Commission special permit may allow transfer to an adjacent lot, one across the street, or for a corner lot, another corner at the same intersection.
The purpose for which a building, structure, space or open land is designed, arranged, maintained or occupied.

The use as defined in ZR Section 12-10: any purpose for which a building, structure or open land may be designed, arranged, intended, maintained or occupied, and any activity, occupation, business or operation carried on or intended there.

A structure that keeps soil away from openings in foundation walls, allows proper grading and drainage, and lets sunlight into a below-grade room (basement) that would otherwise need artificial light.

Issued to a licensed contractor after plan approval so construction can begin. DOB licenses many trades and only a registered contractor can do the work; licenses, registrations and certifications aim to keep unqualified people from endangering the public.

Zoning promotes orderly development and separates incompatible uses, such as industrial and residential. The Zoning Resolution is the legal instrument that regulates land use and limits building size, shape, height and setback.
A tract of land where specific zoning rules apply. It need not match a tax lot, can include one or more tax lots, and may hold multiple buildings.

terms.term: WIE (Written in Error Failure to Maintain)
terms.def: Written in Error Failure to Maintain: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

rules.what: Work generally needs a DOB permit. Some minor alterations, ordinary repairs, and replacing faucets, toilets and sinks need no permit and may be done by someone without a license (AC 28-105.4).
rules.penalty: Violations, court appearances, and civil/criminal penalties

rules.what: A project cannot begin until its plans are approved by a DOB Plan Examiner, or accepted if Professionally Certified; objections on disapproved applications must be resolved first.
After plan approval, a work permit is issued to a licensed contractor; only a registered contractor can perform the work.
When permitted work is finished it must be inspected for final sign-off and a work completion notification submitted to DOB.
Required for major buildings, including new buildings, alterations and demolitions 10 stories or more, and facade work on buildings 15 stories or more (BC 3310, AC 28-110.1).
Commissioning is mandatory when permitted equipment exceeds a total heating capacity of 600 kBTU/h.

Spaces where 75 or more people gather need a Place of Assembly Certificate of Operation (PACO). The initial PACO, issued after DOB inspection, lasts one year; renewal requires an annual FDNY inspection (FC 105.6).
Architectural details may project no more than three inches into the public right of way as-of-right under the Building Code.
A sidewalk that differs from DOT's standard material, color, scoring or dimensions requires Public Design Commission approval.

Storm water from all water-resistant surfaces on a property must drain into a public storm or combined sewer, or an on-site private system such as a drywell; sidewalk and roadway runoff along the frontage must go to a street drainage system.
Excavation work requires coordination with FDNY.
Where the Zoning Resolution is modified by BSA, an approved BSA resolution with BSA-stamped plans is required before DOB review proceeds (ZR 72-00).

rules.rule: Loft Law work in IMD buildings
rules.what: Owners must get a Letter of No Objection from the Loft Board before a permit for work not directly related to IMD units, and Loft Board certification before a permit for work to legalize IMD units.
Occupants may not exceed the number on the Certificate of Occupancy or allowed by BC 1004.1; FDNY may act where crowding or blocked exits threaten safety.
